svg.text: RC422Dev HDLC breadboard: BREADBOARD through your flipped cable (numbers as printed on your board)

Three boards: A = DB-25 connector board, B = four MAX485 modules, C = Pico + level shifter. Green = TX (Pico to ND), blue = RX (ND to Pico), orange = strap. Amber tags [A1]... mark assumptions (listed at the bottom).
numbers = as printed on your DB-25 board
To the ND (sent by the Pico)
From the ND (heard by the Pico)
A / B are the module's screw terminals [A2]
[A4] M4 clock wires cross: A from pin 24, B from pin 11
Power: Pico VBUS (5 V) to the level shifter VCCB and to VCC of all
four modules. Pico 3V3 to VCCA and OE. One common ground:
DB-25 pin 6, all modules, level shifter, Pico. [A3]
- ND tables (service handbook Vol II): section 2-20 page 7 of 8 (HDLC card) and section 2-22 page 5 of 5 (MEGALINK card): pin names, pairs, plus/minus signs, cable pairs.
- The manual's computer-link cable swaps the clock pair (printed 11 to 8, 24 to 21); data and busy go plus to plus. Board B hears the clock on the same pin pairing as the old receiver (A on pin 24).
- Firmware (src/sync.cpp, src/sdlc.pio): TX data GP14, TX clock GP15, RX data GP16, RX clock GP17. Data is read on the rising edge of the clock pin.
- Old breadboard, as you reported it: drivers on pins 23/10 and 21/8, receivers on 25/12 and 24/11, (plus the four plug straps, shown on Board A).

[A1] Pin numbers are as printed on your board. Your AliExpress cable is flipped, so these are NOT the ND's pin numbers. Use HDLC-PCB-ESP32-Wiring.svg for the PCB. Ground on 6 follows from the flip and is not tested.
[A2] On a MAX485 module, A is the plus (non-inverting) wire and B the minus. Check the labels on your modules and the MAX485 datasheet.
[A3] Level shifter channels 5 and 6 for the receive side, OE tied to 3.3 V, and the 5 V supply taken from the Pico VBUS. The old cables on GP16 and GP17 go nowhere.
[A4] Receive clock: A on pin 24, B on pin 11, copied from the old receiver wiring. It is not proven that a real ND needs this.

[A5] The jumpers are what the 3015 card's cable plug has. 9 and 22 are also the MEGALINK's busy-input pins, so this board suits the 3015 only; for a MEGALINK, take the jumpers on 9 and 22 off. Not verified that the ND needs the jumpers.
Not drawn: the 120 ohm termination jumper on each module, surge protection.
JUMPER WIRES - why they are there (names from the ND manual, valid only if [A1] is right)
- Fact: the manual's cable for the 3015 (325402) has these jumpers inside each plug. This board plugs straight into the ND with no cable, so on this PCB the jumpers stand in for that plug.
- Jumpers 9-11 and 22-24: they join the ND's clock output (11, 24) to an input pair on the ND (9, 22). The 3015 manual calls that input 'indication'. So the ND hears its own clock on it.
- Why the cable does that: the pages I read do not say. GUESS, not verified: in computer-link mode the card wants a signal on that input, and the cable supplies one from its own clock.
- Jumpers 3-15-16 and 17-4: the manual lists them as jumper points only. What they do is not documented on the pages read. NOT KNOWN.
- Only a test settles it: build without the jumpers and see if the link comes up. If it does not, add them one strap at a time.

- Still no link: swap plus and minus on ONE pair at a time (data or clock), one change per try, and watch what the ND does. Swapping a pair should be safe for the chips (general knowledge, not checked). Clock polarity is already uncertain [A4].
- Evidence: manual section 2-20 page 7 of 8 (jumpers 3-5, 15-17, 11-24-23, 22-10 in the manual's own numbers) and your beep test, which found exactly these four groups.
